Subsequently, various properties of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps are examined in relation to these new definitions. Notably, both continuous and quasicontinuous mappings can be viewed as special instances of quasicontinuous maps. The study also establishes closed graph and quasicontinuity preservation theorems for composition and inverse images of quasicontinuous maps, respectively.

The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to two
independent thermal reservoirs with different temperatures and energies. We observe
that, as periodic driving forces increase, the system's steady-state becomes drive-dependent 
and it is possible to generate a continuous flow of photons,
naturally resulting from this process. We also demonstrate that this phenomenon 
is fully explained by a theoretical model in the Markovian regime.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. Although studies on base p/q have been conducted, these systems are unusual because their digit sets begin at zero. In contrast, base p/q systems skip over words representing non-positive integers. This paper demonstrates that any set recognisable through p/q-based language analysis can be mapped to a recognisable set in the traditional base p/q system.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while being simple and minimal in its structure. In this study, we thoroughly analyze the associated parameter space, focusing on distinct parameter regimes that arise from the interconnected nature of axion and neutrino parameters. We particularly examine a multi-component dark matter scenario consisting of axions and sterile neutrinos. Under a broader axis-neutrino framework, we also consider a dark matter candidate comprising both axions and sterile neutrinos that does not align with the natural consequences of linking these two sectors. Instead of adhering to a unified axis-neutrino concept, such a disconnected dark matter scenario is plausible and achievable with a significantly broader parameter space. Furthermore, it is important to acknowledge that alternative "axion-or-sterile-neutrino" type frameworks could also successfully describe both DM and baryon asymmetry.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 777,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio $\gtrsim$ 5. On the other hand, the medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 141.4 hours over 53.6 nights and resulted in around 471,000 spectra with a high signal-to-noise ratio $\gtrsim$ 15. This study also involved a detailed examination of the data to ensure its quality. The research team utilized various methods to estimate the physical properties of the stars including the stellar effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$), metallicity ([Fe/H]), and stellar surface gravity ($\log g$). The findings showed that the stars spanned a broad spectrum of characteristics and the results were consistent with expected ratios of elemental composition. This study also highlighted the potential of the data to support time-domain domain research and around 271 Mb of data is publicly accessible through the LAMOST database.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously and providing edge-focused guidance via a residual connection. In experiments conducted on multiple medical image datasets, the results reveal that the EG-CNN module not only boosts segmentation precision but also accelerates training while causing minimal additional computational demands or design modifications, when compared to baseline models.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific, non-consecutive, and alternating coefficients for these functions, confirming a conjecture by Hogbe-Natchon and Quilafon (2020). Additionally, we provide an expression for the Egecioglu-Remmel sequence (1990) and a new interpretation for certain coefficients involving the descent algebra of symmetric groups, extending previous findings by Solus-Toulisse (2019) and Solus-Naruse (2019).

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that manages memory and labels perceptions based on a contrastive change in knowledge. This internal system is characterized as a parametric policy that draws from an internal model and optimizes for an option value, which guides it to reutilize information and discard perceptions that yield suboptimal outcomes. We further explore whether this system can emerge from a world model that uses a hindsight summarization approach and a differential learning method.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and be contributed to by the sun escaping back into space is about 40 percent of the total. However, this contribution varies and depends on whether a coronal mass ejection is involved. When there's no coronal mass ejection, the energy flux contributing to the solar surface is about 3 to 4 times 10 to the power of -5 to -6 watts per square meter, but it jumps to about 11 to 17 times 10 to the power of -5 to -6 watts per square meter in the presence of a coronal mass ejection. These findings are crucial for helping to map the path the solar wind takes and understand the processes that occur as it travels to the solar surface and back out into space.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not suggest any changes in the crystal structure of BFTO up to 6 GPa.  However, a significant reduction in the net magnetic moment was observed, as indicated by Mössbauer spectroscopy when 6 GPa of pressure was reached.  A theoretical analysis using the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker method with a virtual crystal approximation revealed that Bi$_5$BFTO exhibits complex magnetic behavior in the absence of pressure, underlied by magnetic moments of the B and T sites operating in a metastable magnetic state, and biased by magnetic pressure towards an all-in/all-out magnetic phase transition.  Mössbauer spectroscopy at 4.2 K did not provide definitive evidence of magnetic ordering in Bi$_5$BFTO in the absence of pressure, but indicated the possible existence of short-range magnetic interactions below 12 K.  Conversely, in high pressure conditions (above 6 GPa), the possible emergence of magnetic order was enhanced as a result of increased magnetic interactions as suggested by Mössbauer spectroscopy.  This finding is corroborated by our spin-lattice formalism calculations indicating the possible development of weak magnetic order as a result of increased magnetic interactions induced by high pressure.

Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models. These findings hold regardless of the vessel's expansion rate inside the void, though differences arise due to the vessel's wall movement.

Using 18 inverse femtobarns of luminosity from the LHCb experiment, a measurement has been made of the differential decay rate for $B_s^0 \to D_s^{*-} \mu^+ \nu_{\mu}$ across different dimuon invariant mass ranges. By analyzing 2594 events, the differential decay rates were determined in four distinct $D_s^-$ resonant mass intervals. Our results provide constraints on hadronic form factors that can be utilized in future experiments to investigate beyond the Standard Model physics, particularly in searches for $D_s^{-} \to \mu^{-}\bar{\nu}_{\mu}$ rare decays.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, comprising both odd and even degrees. The process of calculating the monodromy matrix for the generalized Hermite polynomials is then undertaken to identify precise conditions under which the potential exhibits monodromy-free characteristics. These conditions are expressed in terms of the coefficients of polynomial roots and can be utilized to predict the number of bound states for (N-1) quantum anharmonic oscillators, where N is the number of roots. This investigation extends findings by prior researchers who observed that certain Schrödinger operators with potential properties corresponding to standard Hermite polynomials are solvable, despite the potential not being a polynomial function.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified.

In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing measurements of a single JJ versus that same JJ within an asymmetrical SQUID loop, where T* can be fine-tuned through applied magnetic flux.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts.

By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fill, constrained by a linear equation determined by the matrix's constraint operator. The analysis extends to multiple phases, various growth conditions, and different elasticity theories, such as Kirchhoff plates and beams. The differential constraints on the fill's substance are derived from the formal scalar capacity estimates of Zhikov.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies, utilizing near-infrared imaging data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam. Our analysis focused on determining the flux fraction of tidal features and influenced galaxies' morphological characteristics. Subsequently, we employed an automated system to identify potential tidal structures in 59200 galaxies and estimated the prevalence of such features in 14200 of them across a wide mass-hue diagram between redshifts 0.05-0.09. Our data revealed that galaxy mergers are most frequently observed in high-mass systems situated in the "near-infrared dropout" region, characterized by prominent tidal structures extending beyond 3 effective radii. Our findings also indicated that tidal structures are more common in galaxies with central stellar populations that have not yet reached the stage of massive stellar collapse. Our data further revealed that tidal structures are symmetric in high-mass galaxies but asymmetric in lower-mass galaxies. Utilizing an automated system to identify tidal structures in a wide field of view, we estimated that the prevalence of mergers in massive galaxies is nearly 10 percent, which is significantly higher than what previous studies have indicated, and it declines by an order of magnitude across a wide range of redshifts. Our data also revealed that tidal structures surrounding mergers are typically similar in radius to those surrounding stable galaxies. Our estimation of tidal features in massive galaxies, which are located beyond 3 effective radii, resulted

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to prioritize less advantaged individuals with moderate potential over advantaged individuals with guaranteed success. The result can vary from guaranteed opportunities to economic analysis of probability thresholds based on specific circumstances. A short-term focused approach, on the other hand, leads to a simpler policy but causes social mobility to stagnate.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques, and demonstrate its capabilities by simulating pulse evolution in a real laser system. Incorporating the FDA for measuring system parameters, this model paves the way for advanced data analytics and potential implementations in inverse design of high-power CPA lasers.

We maintain fixed $p$ and $q$ values, and a dimension reduction theorem is proved which asserts the existence of linear projections from an incompressible set, $K$, from $\ell_p^n$ to $\ell_q^m$, with specific constraints. These constraints indicate that for sufficiently large $n$, there exist projections of a constant factor $\varepsilon > 0$ that reduce the dimension of $K$ by a significant amount, and as $m$ decreases, the projection $\Pi$ becomes closer to being an isometry. Moreover, they highlight a connection between the minimal log-symmetry constant, $MLT_p^n$, and the Tsirelson property of $\ell_p^n$. It is also shown that if $\ell_p^n$ has a low-dimensional incompressible subset, $K$, for all subsets, $K \subset \ell_p^n$, and $n \geq m$, and if $\ell_p^n$ does not contain a certain type of subspace, $l_p^k$, and $k \gg (\log m)^C$, and if $p \notin \{1, 2\}$, and if $p \in \{1, 2\}$, and if $k \gg m^{C}$, and if $p \notin \{1, 2\}$, and if $p \in \{1, 2\}$, and if $k \gg

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in cosmological research. However, this method is limited by systematic errors resulting from instrument noise that can mimic signals from primordial gravitational waves. To accurately characterize future experiments and identify subtle sources of systematic errors influencing current and upcoming measurements of the cosmic microwave background power spectrum and spectral distortion of large-scale structure, full simulation packages are necessary. We have developed the $s4cmb$ Python library to facilitate the simulation of simulated large-scale structure and microwave sky data sets for multiple simulated experiments based on the $s4$ and $cmbspec$ simulation packages. In addition to enabling the simulation of data sets, $s4cmb$ allows for the straightforward application of multiple cosmic microwave background experiments' instrumental systems to simulated data sets, thereby allowing researchers to explore data processing and analysis pipelines and identify subtle sources of systematic errors.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that an malicious entity can implement the attack with just homodyne detection, bypassing the security measures in place. Our findings demonstrate that the attack yields substantial gains, outperforming other attacks by a considerable margin, even surpassing the systems own random noise by a considerable factor. Our research underscores the critical necessity for implementing source phase randomization to a greater degree and determining the minimum level required for the source phase randomization. Moreover, our study proposes modified security protocols that take this new type of attack into account.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Consider a number field K of degree n, with ring of integers O_K and a basis B = (b_1,...,b_n). Let M be the R-lattice formed by the ring O_K within the vector space spanned by B. Building on prior work, we establish an inequality for the successive minima λ_i of (M, B) relative to some norm ||. Specifically, we prove that for any such lattice and norm, λ_i^2 is less than or equal to 2 sum of the square roots of the products of the volumes of the lattice subsets sum_{j=1 to i-1} d_i^2/ Vol(M)/ Vol(M/_i M), where M/_i M denotes the closure of the sublattice formed by the elements of M with norm less than or equal to λ_i. This inequality has implications for studying curves, as it suggests that for curves of genus g, the ratio of the successive minima of the ring of integers of a two-dimensional abelian field with respect to the Grigoriev-Neron model, d_g/d_{g+1}, is bounded by 2+4/g, thus approaching 2 as the genus increases.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for determining pressure. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment over a pressure range (1-1.5 bar), the method effectively captures intricate pressure variations resulting from nitrous gas interacting with a solid surface in various states of flow. Notably, it can also detect very fine-scale pressure differences arising from the conversion of kinetic energy into pressure as well as distinct O2/N2 patterns formed by turbulent mixing processes.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit a rich behavior, with both an insulating property at the bulk and conductivity on the edge. While previous studies have focused on charge modes contributing to edge conductance, recent experiments have revealed non-Abelian and fermionic neutral modes that are expected to display unique dynamics. A theoretical analysis based on a non-Abelian Streda approach has now shown that neutral modes are capable of generating charge currents at the boundary, resulting in dc signals that are distinguishable from thermal contributions and potentially observable using DC measurements. Additionally, upstream neutral modes were found to have longer lifetimes compared to their charged counterparts, providing an explanation for experimental evidence of persistent interference patterns in QCPCX experiments.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization problem and considering neighboring communication constraints, we transform the problem into an easier cooperative optimization issue with reduced complexity. To solve this problem, we introduce an efficient and robust decentralized robust stochastic gradient algorithm, which is distribution-aware and ensures privacy by not directly using local data distributions. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for our proposed algorithm and confirm its effectiveness and robustness distributionally in experiments.

We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of determining the hard-disk pressure has been significantly understated and that the intricate dynamics of this system have also been overlooked. Our study involves a thorough presentation of hard-disk simulation methods, specifically focusing on calculating the equation of state and displaying single-particle properties in detail. Given that previous attempts to measure the hydrodynamic diameter of proteins using simulations have been flawed, our research may also offer valuable insights for this application.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated using Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored.

This research undertakes a detailed examination of Forsage, a pyramid scheme
implemented through Ethereum smart contracts that have attracted significant
investment from cryptocurrency enthusiasts. Despite Forsage's code undergoing a public
audit and its value fluctuating with cryptocurrency prices, it continues to deceive
potential victims by presenting a false sense of security. Due to Ethereum's design,
recovering lost funds becomes nearly impossible once the contract is ruled void. As a
result, pyramid schemes have found a unique platform to thrive within the blockchain
sector. This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of Forsage's architecture,
utilization patterns, and economic dynamics through the investigation of on-chain
data and a crawled website. Furthermore, this research identifies four distinct
risk categories associated with Ethereum investments, categorizing them into
technological, market, governance, and opaque risks.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have utilized the VVV survey to expand the search in the galaxy's bulge region. We have analyzed 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates from Mancini and Giannantonio, utilizing color-magnitude diagrams and radial velocity statistics to evaluate their authenticity. We discovered that 10 of the proposed candidates are true globular clusters, while 9 were either not genuine globular clusters or had previously been identified and removed from the main VVV catalog. Notably, two candidates, GCLMM-08 and GCLMM-19, are particularly significant as they were previously overlooked due to their small size and location in poorly surveyed regions of the sky. We have added these 10 clusters to the VVV catalog, increasing the number of known globular clusters in the galaxy's bulge region. We have also estimated the distance to these clusters, with the majority being around 10 kiloparseks from the galaxy's center. We have also discussed the metallicity of these clusters, with most exhibiting near-solar metallicity. We have also identified two clusters, GCLMM-08 and GCLMM-19, as potentially exhibiting rotation within their nuclei, which could indicate the presence of intermediate metallicity among the galaxy's bulge globular clusters.

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known for their sensitivity to both perturbative and non-perturbative effects. To accurately model differential distributions near their extreme tails, the effective field theory framework of SCET$_{\rm q}$ must consider additional influences, such as mass and power corrections that are equally important. To fully exploit the potential of modern global PDF fits for precision colliders, we need an all-order formalism capable of consistently handling the hierarchy of orders within SCET$_{\rm q}$. In this research, we demonstrate the proof of concept for such an approach by focusing on the Drell-Yan process and specifically, the transverse momentum distribution of lepton pairs, examining the impact of a massive quark in initial states on differential distributions at low transverse momenta. Through the calculation of specific corrections and verification of their balance, we aim to highlight the necessity of a more refined theoretical framework to accurately model differential distributions in this regime.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue. The answer to this sum rule includes a term representing the charge displacement induced by the electric field, which is absent in the dipole-based model but neglected in the velocity-based model. Notably, the displacement current arises from both polarization and quantum geometric effects. Since quantum geometric contributions can be significantly impacted by strong excitations, our TB models must incorporate explicit forms of the Berry connection and curvature. Ultimately, we suggest that the velocity-based method is suboptimal due to its reliance on implicitly compensating effects, which is particularly problematic for

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which are used to approximate quantum error correction codes, specifically networks associated with AdS/CFT and the holographic Earnshaw's theorem. By focusing on networks that maintain symmetry at all levels, we examine their performance in encoding information and how this relates to the properties of boundary systems described by the Haferkamp-Stoermer geometry. However, maintaining bidirectional symmetry in a tensor tree leads to unfavorable correlations that grow rapidly, which contradicts evidence from numerical simulations and theories suggesting that critical multiloop networks should exhibit decaying power-law correlations. To resolve this, a novel network structure called HERMES is created, which utilizes anti-symmetric bonds to ensure linear growth of correlations while maximizing code distance and demonstrating resilience against certain types of noise, which is relevant to tensor network states that represent systems with long decaying power-law correlations.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics of
future process steps. Uniquely, we assess these models under conditions of
limited data due to their high parameter counts. Our key findings suggest that
while deep learning models excel in process prediction when supplied with
substantial, densely annotated event logs, their advantage diminishes under
data scarcity common in real-world scenarios. Notably, under such conditions,
traditional approaches often outperform deep learning models. Consequently,
our analysis suggests that unless process miners have access to large, fully
annotated data sets, traditional methods may be the more suitable choice.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis communication management. Social media can provide valuable information on public sentiment, aiding decision-makers in addressing citizens' primary concerns and adapting communication strategies accordingly. This research aims to assess public opinions expressed on Twitter following the 2020 Izmir earthquake. By analyzing 13,550 tweets collected two weeks after the earthquake, researchers identified key topics such as concern, relief efforts, and infrastructure damage through data mining and topic modeling techniques. The results were visually presented with basic statistics to illustrate public sentiment in the aftermath of the earthquake.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet stellar spectra in a mission that launches in 2022. To address this issue, the Wide-field Survey for Habitable Planets for MetEx, or WiHaPS, is proposed to observe a sample of solar analog and M-dwarf stars in the UV spectrum, which will provide the necessary context for the habitability of these stars and their planets. WiHaPS will contribute to the development of comprehensive stellar flare models by capturing large and small flares across a wide range of stars, which will enable the accurate assessment of stellar activity and the potential habitability of their planets. To demonstrate the significance of wide-field UV surveys in the context of stellar flare modeling, a set of observations were conducted for AD Leo during a large optical flare event, which resulted in a theoretical UV spectrum that closely matched the available IR and X-ray data. While the choice of model impacts the derived UV flux during flare events, future UV data are crucial for reducing this uncertainty, which underscores the importance of wide-field UV surveys for advancing the comprehension of stellar flare composition and the potential habitability

This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's behavior uses mathematical models to derive exact equations describing wave propagation in a finite number of coupled units. Analyzing this through generalized Bloch modes reveals that in the PT-symmetric phase, edge modes arise due to cancellation of phase and PT-symmetry breaking of the effective model, while the PT-broken phase allows for perfect phase and PT-symmetry. Implications for achieving the interaction between absorption and lasing in CPAL devices under active absorption conditions are discussed.

We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult to model the network's behavior over extended periods of time. However, it has been proven possible to transform an self-interacting network into an equivalent network that interacts only between different nodes, which then allows for a more straightforward analysis of its temporal dynamics. This equivalent network exhibits the same behavior and evolution patterns as the original network. Lastly, we develop new algorithms to transfer the mean field and kinetic equations from the original network to its equivalent counterpart. These algorithms, when executed on the transformed network, yield accurate results for the original network. We demonstrate this by applying them to RNA folding models that interact with themselves.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive applications like autonomous driving, however they often struggle with generalization when it comes to geometric transformations, which is crucial for consistent performance. To address this, current methods incorporate geometric smoothing directly into the neural network, which limits their flexibility and efficiency when adapting to different types of transformations. In contrast, our proposed TC framework takes a unique approach by separating geometric smoothing from the neural network and instead applying it to the input data, which not only ensures seamless generalization across various geometric transformations but also allows for easy integration with existing point cloud processors. By doing so, TC achieves a balance between enhanced geometric generalization and minimal performance loss compared to other methods. Our TC framework has shown exceptional generalization across a range of geometric transformations and has also excelled in benchmark evaluations for semantic segmentation and classification.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, integrating them into the OSMAR framework for collaborative interference avoidance. Our simulation results show that ALOHA experiences significant performance degradation due to the cooperative component, whereas CSMA maintains stability across varying network loads, although its collison rates may be initially higher.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both time- and domain-adaptable. We propose a flexible, efficient
encoder framework designed to transform time-indexed embeddings into coherent
temporal relationships. Experimental results on three widely used benchmark
datasets demonstrate that our simple yet effective framework achieves state-of-
the-art performance using off-the-shelf models. Additionally, our work provides
a versatile platform for developing and evaluating novel time-aware models and
knowledge representation techniques.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thereby extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task due to the chameleon nature of the distribution, where the generated text must match both human-like semantics and grammatical correctness. Current work on text generation using GANs is typically limited to small vocabularies, as modeling the full language space with a dense multi-layer perceptron (MLP) generator from a 50k+ word vocabulary would demand an impractically large number of parameters. To address this limitation, we propose the Sparse GAN model, which features an Sparse encoder-style generator that efficiently uses parameters by only considering a subset of relevant vocabulary. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms current state-of-the-art text generation models without requiring the excessively large parameter counts typically associated with GANs.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using galaxy distributions on both small and large scales, which is beyond the capability of traditional perturbation theory. To test the accuracy of our predictions, we employ the HALOCLASS model to compare the PFT results for redshift ranges 0.6 < z < 0.8 and z > 3.0. The discrepancies between the EFT and PT predictions are negligible and should not significantly affect any future galaxy distribution analysis. Furthermore, we investigate the accuracy of foreground removal techniques, specifically using a model of foreground components, and find that they introduce negligible errors. However, we also show that any deviations from accurate galaxy distribution analysis can be effectively removed using precise mass spectrometry.

The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant aspect to consider is the spatial variation in population capture probabilities.  In this study, a new statistical model is developed that integrates telemetry data, occurrence data, and capture data by allowing for individual animal preferences to vary over space and time while accounting for the habitat at capture locations.  This model is initially applied to a wild cat dataset to reveal that cat habitat preferences can differ from their behavior in unobserved areas, as well as how habitat availability impacts capture rates, all of which impact space-use estimates and capture probability curves.  A key contribution of this model is its ability to provide more accurate and reliable inferences on animal behavior in unmonitored areas by addressing potential biases that arise from habitat-related patterns in capture rates and animal movement.  Additionally, a simulation study is conducted to evaluate the model's performance when prey animals exhibit behavior and capture-related patterns not observed in the dataset, and a model is developed to accommodate random effects that capture unobserved variations in animal behavior.

In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking.

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles local and nonlocal vertex communities classification challenges and introduces a novel metric to quantify nodal degrees of freedom. A theoretical framework is developed, combining spectral analysis and information theory, and simulated on eroded random networks to examine spectral and information-theoretic characteristics associated with various vertex communities types. Our findings demonstrate that localized vertex communities, essential for critical transitions, possess lower entropy and more concentrated degree distributions, underscoring the role of localization in shaping dynamic behavior on random networks and potentially, network ensembles. Moreover, our approach effectively differentiates between distinct vertex communities types and outperforms existing methods in classification accuracy.

Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be accomplished through probabilistic imputation methods for assessing player positioning. This study focuses on analyzing the lateral placement of defenders in football during the 2020 European Championship and the 2022 World Cup, employing a generalized valuation method to determine defenders' optimal positions for minimizing scoring opportunities for opponents. A value function representing the probability of conceding a goal in a specific game scenario was utilized to conduct an evaluation of player lateral positioning in international competitions, based on historical data from the 2020 European Championship and 2022 World Cup. Findings from this study were compared to results obtained in a previous study covering the 2018 World Cup finals. Notably, a significant difference was observed in player positioning behavior between tournaments, with a statistical significance of p < 0.05. Furthermore, outcomes for individual teams were also examined, with some teams demonstrating defensive performance levels approaching world-class standards, while others exhibited a significant difference in goal-concession probabilities between tournaments, with a statistical significance of p < 0.01.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the connection of neighboring text segments. Our research indicates that relating text by connecting adjacent segments performs better than clustering-based methods. We also demonstrate that our technique achieves superior results in extracting information from damaged forms in comparison to leading industry techniques.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to behave effectively, with important applications in spectral analysis of random matrix ensembles. However, standard asymptotic freeness, independent of matrix size $N$, requires careful consideration. Traditional asymptotic freeness involves taking limits as $N$ increases, but this approach is not always convenient for certain applications. Instead, we propose understanding asymptotic freeness as a property that emerges between independent unitarily invariant random matrices of differing sizes and shapes. Specifically, we investigate the impact of matrix resizing and provide an explicit expression for expected asymptotic freeness that incorporates two key elements: standard asymptotic freeness and a form of conditional freeness that depends on the distribution of larger matrices given those of smaller ones. This understanding is verified for various unitarily invariant distributions for both classical and non-classical random matrices. Additionally, we introduce a method for estimating the expected asymptotic freeness of unitarily invariant random matrices based on their respective cumulative distribution functions.

We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny.

Determining the extent of polarization within social networks is vital, yet currently, there is no established metric to effectively measure the separation between polarization and noise. Moreover, the comparative performance of various polarization methods remains unclear due to a lack of normalization. To rectify this, we introduce the Polarization Separation Ratio (PSR), a normalized measure that effectively compares the degree of polarization against noise in social networks. PSR leverages the concept of polarization distance and employs the average shortest path for normalization, a common feature in network analysis. Through normalized evaluations using both synthetic and normalized measurements of various polarization methods, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed Polarization Separation Ratio (PSR) over other techniques.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint the test case that discovered the issue and the specific part of the code where the bug resides, thereby aiding in making bug fixes more straightforward.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork, enabling a universal model to be trained to handle an extensive range of tasks. Notably, hyper-prompts are relatively compact, significantly reducing both training and inference costs compared to other task-conditioning methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of HyperPrompt in a multi-task image classification scenario, achieving a 50% reduction in effective batches, a 50% decrease in training memory usage, and a 20% improvement in accuracy, all with just a few hundred additional hyper-prompts.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions between states connected by the dipole interaction, which share the same parity. Our study reveals that parity protection against losses is maximized at specific times when a photon-number distribution shifted by two units is observed, allowing for enhanced even-photon bundle emission through optimized control of an initial state.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for an infinitely scalable network, with constant values for delta and epsilon. Furthermore, the algorithm is efficient in terms of communication, employing a communication cost of O(log^3 (n)) bits per malicious node.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from their intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.
