This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:1609.09321], the study begins with connections associated with a class of adapted differential geometries over Lie groupoids. The study will examine Adjoint Bundle Connections, Homogeneous Bundle Connections, and Higgs Connections, before moving onto more complex concepts. 

Next, the research aims to investigate the gauge transformations of these connections, leading to the introduction of curvature concepts for Morita equivalence of analytic structures on Lie groupoids. It will also introduce connections over coarse moduli spaces of Lie groupoids and prove the existence of canonical Gaussian-Bernstein operators for these connections. Finally, the research intends to introduce and potentially establish a connection over 2-foliations on Lie groupoids.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows and those that are quiescent.  The former exhibit smaller effective radii and higher mass concentrations compared to their silent counterparts.  The median values for compact, dynamic cores are significantly smaller in size - by a factor of 2.5 in width - and represent only a tiny fraction of the total cloud mass.  In contrast, inactive cores display broader dimensions and more substantial proportions of the overall cloud mass.  These findings suggest that the initial formation sites for massive stars lie within the densest, most concentrated regions at the heart of star-forming regions.  The discovery of core growth phenomenon in the dragon infrared dark cloud provides empirical validation for theoretical models suggesting that large-scale collapse is necessary for the birth of massive stars.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature extraction and machine learning algorithms. We tested these methods on a LiDAR dataset from a mixed urban and forested area, and our results show that utilizing 2D orientation features and combining them with local 3D context and spectral data from optical LiDAR significantly improved classification accuracy.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. We discuss the consequences of establishing a second-order differential equation for Gegenbauer polynomials in terms of its ladder operators, and subsequently, the implications for constructing a harmonic analysis on the space of rotation groups. This leads to the development of a Hecke algebra and a model for a spherical Satake isomorphism. Despite having a rich mathematical framework, this system is not directly applicable to the study of random fields on the sphere. We address this limitation by modifying the algebraic structure to remove the differential constraints, and thereby obtaining a model for computing covariance coefficients of a stationary random field on the sphere.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased indication of hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions, building upon existing techniques. Leveraging existing data from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES from 2004 to 2018 and 2007 to 2018 respectively, along with VLT for 11 years, we sought correlations between neutrinos and UHECRs and found no substantial over-densities of UHECR arrival densities within 0.1°-1.0° radii around the positions of high-energy neutrinos. Additionally, we utilized deep learning techniques to enhance the sensitivity of positional UHECR searches, while also introducing two novel approaches: weighting UHECR energies based on neutrino interaction lengths and analyzing the distribution of neutrino shower lengths as a function of UHECR positions within 0.1°-1.0° ranges. This research significantly expands the knowledge base for neutrino-UHECR correlations, offering more stringent constraints on the cosmological origin of neutrinos.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during extension. We observed that the initiation of yield stress during foam film breaking requires a critical value of applied strain, which is directly related to the surface roughness. However, we also found that the maximum stress reached during this process is unaffected by surface roughness. Our results indicate that initial slip at the surface contributes to the tension applied to the foam film, playing a crucial role in determining its stability.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to identify the outlier class. Ultimately, our strategy involved removing uncertain samples and making predictions based on the ensemble's output.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, ultimately dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just primary finger states but also multi-finger states, addressing both primary curvature-driven and tension-driven restorative forces, thereby enabling determination of the state's finger number, length, and thickness. The number of branches observed in the theory align with those seen in the elastic fingering of viscous fluids previously studied. Elongation factor data for short fingers are collected and show a distinct transition at a critical ratio, indicating the onset of a multi-finger branch. The study's findings may have value in understanding subsurface processes like salt finger convection and the formation of geological structures.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, ethynyl cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, TMC-1, a submillimeter molecular cloud, through observation. Using model analysis, researchers have concluded that a model is ethynyl cyclopentadiene, comprising approximately 1 percent of total carbon, while another model, comprising approximately 4 percent of total carbon. These findings are consistent with carbon usage but contradict the abundance of nitrogen which is estimated to be seven to eight times 10 to the power of -5. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene abundencies are surprising given that cyclopolyaromatic hydrocarbon species, such as cyclooctatriene, have been previously detected in TMC-1. The formation of small nitrogen deficiency cycles, such as cyclooctatriene and ethynyl cyclopentadiene, may be favored by atom recombination barriers, providing a potential explanation for this phenomenon.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to bridge the dark matter and dark energy phases, making it an interesting area of study. We derived the necessary conditions for the existence of both matter- and cosmological constant-like solutions in both expanding and contracting universes, and these conditions were then used to estimate the density and viscosity of the fluid in its different phases. Through a combination of semi-analytical and numerical methods, we were able to determine the evolution of the density and temperature of the fluid over time and this evolution was presented in graphical form. Our results showed that the model is physically viable, with density decreasing during the dark matter phase and increasing during the dark energy phase, in line with observations. Furthermore, the model can explain the transition from one phase to another and this is presented graphically.

In educational settings, curiosity is a vital cognitive trait that fuels desire for knowledge and fuels effective learning.  However, because curiosity is subjective and varies from person to person, it remains a significant challenge to accurately measure and gauge its intensity during learning experiences.  What's more, because curiosity is inherently multimodal and drawn from multiple sources, a singular analytical method falls short of capturing its complexity.  To tackle this problem, we present an original and comprehensive approach that integrates both textual and visual elements to analyze the complexity of ideas and visual engagement in a learning setting.  Our framework utilizes both self-reported data and implicit indicators of visual attention to quantify idea complexity and visual engagement.  Through experiments involving 21 small groups who utilized a collaborative learning tool to learn about cells, we show that our approach successfully captures curiosity's fluctuating and dynamic nature, while also highlighting the distinct differences between curiosity expression in solitary and joint learning settings.  Furthermore, we demonstrate how our approach stress-tests curricula designed to stimulate curiosity, identify patterns of idea interaction that reflect curiosity, and identify group members who are more curious.  To build on our proposed solution, we discuss potential applications of our approach in educational contexts.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space to its benefit, it enables interdependence between sample points beyond the immediate neighbors.  While employing a nearest neighbor covariance model would restrict the reachable Mat\'ern classes to $\nu \leq 0.25$, it presents an insurmountable challenge for applications seeking smoother functions.  This study introduces an augmentable likelihood for the Mat\'ern covariance model that is applicable to any base graph, it enables it to be integrated within the broader integrated nested Laplace approximation family for efficient and scalable Bayesian inference.

The effective management of urban roads banks heavily on timely and accurate real-time monitoring of traffic conditions. Although deploying numerous sensors can optimize traffic management systems, continuously monitoring conditions with a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles presents a more cost-effective solution with added benefits of data collection. Unfortunately, determining the smallest possible vehicle fleet that can efficiently sense the entire road network remains a challenging task due to its significant dependence on unpredictable traffic patterns. This problem of optimal sensing by a minimal fleet of sensing vehicles with unknown traffic remains largely unexplored. To address this problem, we propose a modeling approach using robust optimization to capture the variability of urban road networks. By formulating and simplifying a mathematical model for vehicle sensing, we can efficiently solve even large-scale problems. Our proposed method involves a dual approach that combines a heuristic solution and a method of optimal rounding. Through simulations, we demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm over randomly selected alternatives. Furthermore, our results showcase the effectiveness of our algorithm in significantly reducing unnecessary sensor usage while reducing computational time by several orders of magnitude.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle's rare and experimentally unobserved decay into visible gamma rays and invisible particles for various hypothetical neutrino and dark matter interactions described by effective field theories. By placing stringent limits on these interactions, we utilize existing J/ψ decay data from the Belle experiment to infer possible values for dark matter's absolute mass and its relationship to neutrinos in the so-called J/ψ bump, a range of approximately 1 GeV to 1.2 GeV. Our findings suggest that if dark matter interacts with nucleons through neutrinos, its coupling strength could be as high as certain two-body interaction rates allow. If sterile neutrinos with a mass between 0.0001 eV and 0.0066 eV exist and interact with dark matter, we successfully close all previously allowed, narrow ranges for them based on the Belle's data, including a 0.0029 eV to 0.0066 eV range indicated by observations of the J/ψ bump in cosmic neutrino spectra from the Milky Way's dwarf spheroidal galaxies.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these systems can be manipulated, but the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplained. This study aims to shed light on the intricate nature of AES systems by examining their vulnerability to subtle shifts in input data. Through the use of statistical analyses and controlled experiments, we've discovered that these systems are highly sensitive to minute changes, resulting in significant discrepancies between automated scores and actual grades assigned by human educators. Moreover, we've identified that the vocabulary used by these systems' components plays a pivotal role, making them susceptible to undue influence. To mitigate this vulnerability, we've proposed a straightforward yet effective strategy to make the algorithms more robust. This method demonstrates a notable reduction in the magnitude of score distortion when faced with data manipulation, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of these machine learning-based scoring systems.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode. A study was conducted to证实 this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle density profiles. It was discovered that increasing a magnetic field allows access to the helicon mode, distinguished by a central high-density region, and characterized by enhanced particle density and momentum transport rates.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While gold-standard pathologic analysis relies on expert interpretation of whole slide images, it's hindered by time-consuming processes, high expenses, and personnel requirements. To accommodate rising cancer diagnoses, a computer-aided system that can identify and analyze malignant cells from histopathology images is essential for this task. However, accurately detecting and classifying nuclei in H&E stained images remains a challenge due to the vast number of nuclei, the presence of overlapping cells, and the variability among nuclei. To address the issue of nucleus localization, we propose a novel whole slide image segmentation network called Nucleus Detection Network (N-WNet), which builds on the concept of initial nucleus prediction from image patches. For an extensive dataset of 80 whole slide images from eight different histopathology reports, our model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in segmenting nuclei, outperforming both traditional image processing methods and other deep learning approaches. As a result, this proposed computer-aided diagnosis method provides a robust and efficient means of analyzing histopathology images to detect and classify nuclei.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's response to intracellular damage signals, primarily the gasdermin E protein.  To understand the cellular mechanisms behind pyroptosis, we created a single-cell model that simulates various aspects of GDE activation.  Our model reveals the interconnection between NLRP3 and GDE, as well as the varying effects of NLRP3 inhibitors, anti-inflammatory drugs, and virus replication on the inflammatory response and cell lysis.  Specifically, we found the timing of NLRP3 inhibition has a minimal effect on the cell's survival, but the intensity of the DIDS treatment significantly impacts the cell's outcome.  In addition, we observed that limited virus replication can actually strengthen the inflammatory response, likely due to the increased stress it places on the cell.  By leveraging this single-cell modeling approach, we can gain valuable insights into the complex cellular mechanisms underlying COVID-19 and other infectious diseases, which can ultimately inform the development of more effective therapeutic interventions.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that the agent can control. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables is established, enabling the agent to ignore the uncontrollable variables and concentrate on the key variables that matter the most. This topic is further explored by applying necessary and sufficient conditions for factoring Markov decision processes to an actual robotics learning scenario, where an agent is tasked with learning to navigate an environment that is subject to external influences occurring at a specific time.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined feature patterns, derived from the Laplacian matrix. This aligns with the widely accepted DNN view, while our matched filter theory uniquely identifies specific layers responsible for pattern matching and allows for innovative design choices, such as separately matching different patterns across GCNNs' parallel branches. Distinguishing ourselves from previous explanations, our approach provides a clear mathematical foundation that connects GCNNs to GC regression techniques. We validate and leverage our findings that GCNNs' matched filter behavior may result in suboptimal performance when using common graph convolutional methods, as these often force unrelated feature patterns to be matched during data transformation. We experimentally support our hypotheses and demonstrate how our insights can be applied to create more effective GCNNs by explicitly designing matching mechanisms for specific feature patterns.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is combined with a complex scalar field in the presence of a U(1) gauge field, resulting in a 'hairy' black hole phenomenon. A particular set of 'hairy' black holes is found to be thermodynamically equivalent to ordinary black holes, and all show identical external properties. Nevertheless, internal structures reveal distinct, spiral-shaped patterns. A discrete set of scalar field configurations, representing non-singular solitons, is also identified. These configurations are shown to represent smooth, deformed versions of rotating cylinders. The configuration of both the 'hairy' black holes and the solitons is derived using a three-dimensional Chern-Simons-type action, establishing a direct relationship between them.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited sampling rate restricts its application. A novel approach, the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique, offers improved lateral resolution and signal-to-noise ratio by combining the methods. This research introduces a theoretical framework and simulation models for the VSSA method, demonstrating its potential to enhance lateral displacement estimation through lower interpolation error. Furthermore, the proposed approach allows for increased interpolation order without interference with data processing. Although requiring increased data storage, the VSSA method allows accessing high-resolution SA beams with lower interpolation error, resulting in more precise lateral displacement estimation.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

The concept of Boolean Ramsey numbers for sets of posets was initially explored in relation to Boolean lattices and posets obtained from chains with minimal elements combined into a V-shaped structure. A key objective is to establish a minimum number 'n' for any number of color options where a given V-shaped poset will be entirely colored with a specific color in a Boolean lattice. Recent work has led to the determination of Boolean Ramsey numbers for specific instances, and this paper aims to build on that by investigating the Boolean Ramsey numbers for V-shaped posets and identifying them for more complex structures and one additional structure of a different poset type. Additionally, a method is provided for calculating a lower bound for the V-shaped poset Boolean Ramsey numbers using a technique involving a transformation of posets and previous mathematical findings.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target number $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist specific events, $A_i$, with individual probabilities matching the elements $x_i$, such that the combined probability of events occurring in a sequence ($P(\bigcup_{j=1}^n A_{i_j})$) is maximized or minimized based on their cyclic order, and 'nontransitive' when the combined probability is solely influenced by the sequence, and we investigate the structure of these 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' sets, and it is shown that both types can be expressed as closed sets, and the set of 'nontransitive' points is compact, and the measure of 'nontransitive' points is infinite, and the compactness of 'nontransitive' points is shown for n=3, and we also consider events with dependent relationships, and the compactness of 'nontransitive' points is shown for n=3, and it is established that almost all n-tuples are capable of modeling Dependent Cyclic events, and the compactness of 'nontransitive' points is shown for n=3, and it is established that almost all n-tuples are capable of modeling Dependent Cyclic events, and the set of 'nontransitive' points is shown to be homeomorphic to specific poly

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in improving the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose reference images. However, the use of mean absolute error in the reverse cycle has been found to cause issues, often resulting in output images that resemble the training data rather than providing optimal enhancement. To address this limitation, we propose a new cycleGAN framework based on AdaSwitch, which replaces the traditional loss function and allows for more effective and adaptable training. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on several public datasets, and when combined with perceptual loss, it also excels in a private clinical dataset. For comparison, AdaSwitch can also be viewed as an improved version of the original cycleGAN approach.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine unlabeled data's representations. The experiments show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art results significantly. The code will be made available at https://github.com/ghy1999/SPACE-2.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when coupled with a torsion-forming vector field and the relationship between the 
conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric and the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first 
derive conditions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a state of 
expansion, stability, or contraction. Subsequently, we establish a Laplace 
equation using the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe soliton when the soliton's potential 
vector field is a gradient type. Additionally, this research relates an ideal 
fluid's spacetime to a Robertson-Walker spacetime and discusses various physics 
and gravitational implications.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and super-resolution security at video level detection and removal challenges.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate and form coherent weak boson beams at the $W$ and $Z$ resonance, a novel approach known as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation (EVBA) has been developed. In contrast to the conventional VBBA, which treats the particle in question as a weak boson, EVBA separates the weak boson into its components. This approach is particularly useful for studying parton-to-parton interactions where one of the participants is a weak boson. We develop and apply a parton distribution function (PDF) formalism for EVBA calculations, utilizing a Python-based module called EVBApy. This development is performed within the context of muon colliders but can be applied to any high-energy lepton collider. Furthermore, we compare EVBA and VBBA predictions for both diagonal and off-diagonal parton-to-parton scattering processes at $\sqrt{s}=10$ TeV.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
mechanism is commonly used in model-based learning methods, using a single shared
model for multiple tasks raises the risk of cross-task interference, potentially
compromising the benefits multi-task learning is supposed to provide. In this study,
we show that separating the sub-functions of the model into distinct, task-specific
components allows each sub-function to generalize effectively, even when these
elements are stochastic. Building on this finding, we derive theoretical bounds
that demonstrate how this approach can significantly reduce interference, particularly
in models storing transition and reward information. In our experiments using a
corporate learning framework, our proposed method showed significant improvements
over existing models using a single shared dynamics and reward function, showing
clear evidence of decreased interference and better performance.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within a annular region in Clifford analysis.

When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed for a two-hop, time-division multiple access system, which leverages reinforcement learning to optimize beam selection in the second hop. Notably, this approach does not necessitate prior knowledge of channel conditions or performance statistics, and instead focuses on a joint beam training strategy aimed at maximizing overall communication performance through a reinforcement learning framework. A multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient approach is implemented to develop optimized beam training patterns and, through both theoretical analysis and computer simulations, it is shown that this approach results in significant reductions in total training time and substantial improvements in overall system performance.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, it uses a multi-headed feedforward network to model complex periodic signal components and encode latent codes for a regressive model. Secondly, it employs a dilated convolution neural network that adapts to periodicity as part of KPNet, serving as both a decoder and query-by-frequency model. Experimental evaluations on the LibriSpeech corpus demonstrate the effectiveness of qPNet in producing quasi-periodic audio signals with a Markov order of 12 and a model size of 89.44M parameters.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this interface and present results from
an experiment conducted with the system.

Planets located in the habitable zones of F, A, and B-type stars face intense stellar ultraviolet radiation, which significantly alters their atmospheric composition through photochemical reactions. These reactions can either accumulate destructive molecules like ozone or oxygen, potentially offering protection against further damage, and can also facilitate the creation of notable organic compounds, including nitrogen hydrides, nitrogen dioxide, and nitrogen triiodide. To understand how this solar ultraviolet radiation impacts low-mass exoplanets, a comprehensive photochemical model has been applied to nitrogen-rich, temperate worlds, small super-earths, and large gas giants. This modeling reveals distinct photochemical responses based on their stellar host characteristics and internal temperatures, which may be observable through spectral analysis.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic defect detection and marking analysis. To expedite and reduce costs associated with manual inspections, a comprehensive system called RoadAtlas has been developed, providing a holistic solution encompassing road flaw detection, marking parsing, interactive data visualization through a web interface, and a robust database framework supported by API tools.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Notably, it also excels in more demanding scenarios, where the sound source is not always visible in the video.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version, and introduces a Lorentzian normalisation to ensure effective information propagation. LGCN demonstrates superior performance on synthetic and real-world datasets for node classification tasks, and its ability to uncover tree-structured patterns makes it a valuable tool for visualising and analysing complex networks.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

A new method has been created that successfully transfers squeezed states into optical cavities even in stable conditions. The method builds upon conventional optomechanical setups, utilizing a three-level atom to facilitate the transfer. Two techniques were devised to observe the squeezed state transfer effect, including applying a controlled influx of squeezed phonons and simulating the system in an environment of phonon-squeezed vibrations. Our model demonstrates the ability to efficiently achieve this transfer in optomechanical systems.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets comprised of fundamental elements and investigate its core properties. The complexity of model verification can be resolved for orbit-finite structures, and a parallel connection with parity games exists. In contrast, the issue of determining satisfaction becomes insoluble. Additionally, the limitations of modal $\mu$-calculi with enriched atoms are identified, and we explore how the expressive potential of these systems depends on both the arrangement of these atoms and whether a basic or composite syntax is employed.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, inspired by 2001 data from Miller and Eisenberg.
Our analysis of these data indicates that traditional assumptions regarding
decreasing tolerance as tolerance increases do not hold, leading to
proposed alternatives including the effectiveness and entropy of information
and demonstrating that higher desirability correlates with higher
acceptability via Tsallis entropy when combining these concepts with
bounded rationality. Additionally, we demonstrate that impatience may yield
delay-dependent tolerance, efficacy, and information, ultimately yielding
variable coefficients for the Schrodinger equation and prompting investigation
into their possible correlations.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and homomorphisms. We define the notion of Extended Double Covers (EDCs) in signed graphs and demonstrate through numerous examples that many classes of signed graphs have bounded homomorphism types to exclude a minor pair, specifically K_4- and K_5-EDCs. Additionally, we prove that planar signed graphs are a subset of the K_5-EDC-excludable homomorphism-bounded graphs, and this inclusion is not redundant. Finally, we suggest that research into EDC-minor-excludable homomorphism-bounded graphs may yield promising results.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with weights from {-1,0,1}. The goal of this article is to solve the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where $|A|$, when A is a set of integers, and investigate the underlying structure of A to achieve this minimum value. Additionally, some open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ are proposed in this article.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external and periodically varying sources.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed low water content and normal to enriched D/H isotopic composition. Analyzing Benenitra and Chelyabinsk samples revealed three distinct water populations with varying D/H isotopic signatures, suggesting that IAB and H chondrites may not accurately reflect the water content of early asteroid parent bodies. Instead, it is proposed that "wet" and "dry" planetesimals with mixed water contents, resembling modern CI chondrites, were more common in the inner solar system.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any magnon root, regardless of its degeneracy. We verify these results with spin-3/2 XXZ as a test case. Additionally, we observe affine quantum-group symmetry in the form factors.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot speech-to-text translation, which00equals zero-shot speech recognition, translating languages or dialects for which no training data is accessible. We assess the impact of utilizing high-quality text-to-speech (TTS) data for training purposes, yielding surprising findings indicating zero-shot speech-to-text translation performance surpassing zero-shot speech recognition when utilizing high-quality TTS data. We observe that models utilizing speech input learn both speech-to-text (ST) and TTS mappings to an expanded central representation encompassing all trained languages. To rectify models employing speech input and achieve results comparable to text-based approaches in zero-shot scenarios, we introduce the concept of prototypical neural machine translation. Our evaluation across eight languages and dialects, including Mandarin, demonstrates utilizing TTS data via prototypical NMT yields substantial gains, notably +10.4 BLEOU, over utilizing speech input directly. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical basis for this technique through analysis of spherical geometry.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian multipoles, Spherical multipoles and Trefftz multipoles. Our findings suggest that Cartesian and spherical expansions are solely appropriate for objects much smaller than the wavelength of the incident light, whereas linearly polarized Trefftz multipoles effectively describe light interaction with targets of any size and any shape. Due to their ability to model curved wavefronts and their Cartesian-based framework, these Trefftz multipoles can be used to accurately calculate optical forces on nanostructures, as opposed to spherical multipoles which fail to do so.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues. Further, infinite row (column) young-capelli bitableaux represent Narasimhan-Ramanujan characters and their duals, respectively.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence theoretical models, particularly those relying on effective low-energy models.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for employing generative adversarial networks to create accurate and reliable medical diagnoses from chest X-rays is explored. To test this, a model based on partial source domain adaptation is trained on the CheXpert dataset to identify eight common lung diseases. After demonstrating satisfactory performance, the generative ISNet network is utilized to visualize how specific disease patterns affect the model and generate chest X-rays that signal those particular conditions. An experimental investigation into source domain robustness is also conducted to assess the model's response to disease patterns in healthy areas of X-rays. A user study with medical professionals is organized to gather their opinions on the disease-aware images and evaluate their source fidelity. Furthermore, a potential application in medical education and patient awareness is discussed.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid-based method like finite differences generates a source term that is precisely known at grid points but unknown elsewhere. In this work, we aim to calculate the potential at any point in the domain rapidly. By representing the potential as a sum of the source distribution and a depth function derived from the distance along normal lines to the boundary, we can accurately approximate the source by using a boundary integral method, specifically the boundary element method (BEM). We can then leverage a fast multipole method (FMM) to solve this efficiently. This approach combines the high precision of BEM for regions with complex boundaries and the computational speed of FMM, enabling its application to large-scale problems on a parallel computer. Numerical experiments demonstrate notable speed improvements over direct Gaussian solvers and other iteration-based methods.
